text.p: The following are some of the leading stories in Finnish papers this morning.
- President Martti Ahtisaari says has no health problems, but would rather keep his weight a secret, like German Chancellor Helmut Kohl.
- The massmedia is losing its traditional role as a public service and playing more to the dictates of business, says International federation of journalists secretary-general Aidan White.
- Kesko has already began seeking buyers for Tuko. Sale could be done either as one deal, or partly to investors as a listed company.
- Merita chief equities analyst Elina Timonen says forest industry's profits and share prices could be hit if Euro currency is strong against the dollar when forestries face recession.

- Co-operative banking group will on Wednesday decide timetable for organisation restructuring seen increasing local co-operative banks' mutual responsibility for losses. Some banks want decision only next spring instead of December as planned.
- Consumer group Hackman Oy Ab's incoming managing director Tapio Hintikka welcomes company's recent decision to increase number of cheaper high-volume products.
- Kleinwort Benson recommends buy for Finnish food, animal feeds and chemicals group Raision Tehtaat Oy, for forestry group UPM-Kymmene Oy and for compass and electronics device maker Suunto Oy.
- Visiting St Petersburg governnor Vladimir Jakovlev condemns Duma's decision to impose extra fees on cargo trucks crossing Russian borders.

- President Martti Ahtisaari says Finland will decide its stance on the issue of next UN Secretary-General only after Security Council has made its decision known to the general assembly. Finland has been on good terms with incumbent Boutros Boutros-Ghali, he says.
- The controversy surrounding Kesko's Tuko acquisition could have been avoided if Finland had its own merger laws, Kesko CEO Eero Kinnunen says.
- Growth in restaurant sales depends more on food sales as people prefer to drink cheap imported alchol at home.
- Experts say new information networks, especially the internet, do not pose a threat to traditional media houses as providers of information.
